Equal
EE-kwal
adj. (the same in measure, worth, or standing; also, fair and even-handed; rendering Hebrew takan, Greek isos)
From Latin aequalis, from aequus, level, even. The KJV carries both senses — identical in degree, as in Christ's equality with the Father, and even-handed, as in the masters' duty to render what is just and equal.

Biblical Definition

Equal in Scripture bears the full metaphysical weight in the Christological texts and a plain ethical weight elsewhere. Paul writes that Christ, “being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2:6) — equality with God was not something snatched at, because it was already His by right; and the humbling that follows is the more astonishing for it. John records the same claim from the hostile side, and the hostility proves the claim was understood: the Jews sought the more to kill Him “because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18). No one present treated this as a metaphor. In the ethical register, Paul lays a duty on masters that was revolutionary in a slaveholding empire: “Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1) — the ground being that the master is himself a servant. Ezekiel meets the complaint of a people who think God unfair: “Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?” (Ezekiel 18:25). And the parable of the labourers turns on the word: the first-hired object that the householder has made the last “equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day” (Matthew 20:12), and the answer is that no one was defrauded — grace given to another takes nothing from you.

Webster 1828 Definition

The same in measure or standing, and also even-handed. Christ's equality with God is His by right; masters owe servants what is just and equal; Ezekiel answers those who call God's way unequal; and the labourers resent an equality that cost them nothing.

expand to see more

EQUAL, a. [L. aequalis, from aequus, even, level.] Having the same magnitude or dimensions; being of the same bulk or extent.

2. Having the same value; being of the same importance.

3. Having the same qualities or condition; as, men are equal in their natural rights.

4. Even; uniform; not variable; as an equal temper.

5. Just; equitable; giving the same or similar rights or advantages. Give unto your servants that which is just and equal. Col. 4.

Key Scripture

Philippians 2:6 — "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:"

John 5:18 — "Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God."

Colossians 4:1 — "Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven."

Ezekiel 18:25 — "Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?"

Modern Corruption

Equality has been converted from a statement about worth and standing into a demand for identical outcomes, so that any difference of role, reward, or result is read as injustice — a premise Scripture answers directly in the parable of the labourers.

expand to see more

Scripture's equality is genuine and radical: every human being bears the image of God; the ground is level at the cross, where there is no difference, for all have sinned; and in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female as to standing and inheritance. What Scripture never derives from that is the identity of roles or the equalisation of outcomes. The same apostle who wrote Galatians 3:28 assigned different offices in the household and the church; the same Lord who declared all men equally guilty distributed talents unequally, five and two and one, and required an account proportioned to what was given. The parable of the labourers is the decisive text because it stages the objection precisely: the complaint is not that anyone was underpaid but that others were treated generously, and the householder's answer is that his eye is good and theirs is evil. Envy dressed as a demand for fairness is an old vice with a new vocabulary.

The Christological texts are corrupted in the opposite direction and with graver consequence. Philippians 2:6 has been rendered so as to make Christ a man who declined to grasp at a divinity He did not possess, and John 5:18 dismissed as the Jews' misunderstanding — the standard route by which Arian and Unitarian readings dispose of the deity of Christ. Neither works. Paul's point requires that Christ already possessed what He did not clutch, or the emptying is empty. And John reports the charge without correcting it, then has Jesus answer at length in a way that heightens rather than reduces the claim: what things soever the Father doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise (John 5:19). The dictionary holds the Nicene confession that the Son is of one substance with the Father, equal in power and glory.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew takan (to weigh, measure, make even — the verb rendered equal in Ezekiel 18:25) and shavah (to be level, equal); Greek isos (equal) and isotes (equality, equity).

expand to see more

Hebrew takan (H8505) — to weigh out, measure, make even; the verb behind the way of the Lord is not equal.

Hebrew shavah (H7737) — to be level, equal, comparable; used in Proverbs 3:15 of nothing being comparable to wisdom.

Greek isos (G2470) — equal, the same; the word in Philippians 2:6, John 5:18, and Matthew 20:12.

Greek isotes (G2471) — equality, equity, fairness; the word in Colossians 4:1 and 2 Corinthians 8:13-14.

Greek harpagmos (G725) — a thing seized or to be grasped at; the noun rendered robbery in Philippians 2:6.

Usage

"“Thought it not robbery to be equal with God” — not snatched at, because already His by right."

"“Making himself equal with God” — the charge is reported and never corrected."

"“Thou hast made them equal unto us” — the complaint of men who lost nothing by another's generosity."
